elements.source: Total body calcium (1000–1300 g) resides in bones to the extent of: [99.3% bones, 0.6% soft tissue, 0.1% ECF. (Book p874)]

Match the soft-tissue calcium fractions — 1) Free (ionized)  2) Bound to albumin  3) Bound to other proteins … A) 40%  B) 12%  C) 48% [Soft-tissue calcium: 48% free ionized, 40% albumin-bound, 12% other proteins. (Book p874)]
The normal corrected calcium range is: [Normal corrected Ca2+ 8.6–10.3 mg/dL. (Book p874)]
Corrected Ca2+ = Total Ca2+ + ___. [Corrected Ca = Total Ca + 0.8 (4 − albumin level). (Book p874)]
Corrected calcium defines hypocalcaemia below and hypercalcaemia above: [<8.4 mg/dL hypocalcaemia; >10.5 mg/dL hypercalcaemia. (Book p874)]

Free ionized calcium functions include sensitizing CaSR, myocyte contractility, neuromuscular activity and: [Functions: sensitize CaSR, myocyte contractility, neuromuscular activity, bone mineralization. (Book p874)]
‘In acidosis, H+ competes with calcium for albumin, raising the free Ca2+.’ [↑ H+ (acidosis) → ↑ free Ca2+; ↓ pH by 0.1 unit → ↑ Ca2+ by 0.1 meq/L. (Book p874)]
A fall in pH by 0.1 unit raises ionized calcium by: [↓ pH 0.1 unit → ↑ Ca2+ 0.1 meq/L. (Book p874)]
Plasma calcium equals: [Plasma Ca = free Ca2+ + Ca2+ complexed to anions. (Book p874)]
Calcium absorption occurs in the proximal small intestine with the order: [Site: proximal small intestine (jejunum > duodenum); ~20% net absorption (~200 mg), enhanced by acid. (Book p874)]

Match absorption route — 1) 95% active transcellular  2) 5% passive paracellular … A) Independent of calcitriol  B) Tightly controlled by calcitriol [95% active transcellular (calcitriol-controlled); 5% passive paracellular (independent). (Book p874)]
Calcitriol drives transcellular calcium absorption by: [Calcitriol binds nuclear receptors, releases calbindin, activates TRPV5/6; calcium exits via Ca2+ ATPase. (Book p874)]

Free ionized calcium functions listed are sensitizing CaSR, myocyte contractility, neuromuscular activity and bone mineralization. Pick the ODD ONE OUT: [Ionized Ca sensitizes CaSR and drives contractility, neuromuscular activity and mineralization — suppression is the odd one. (Book p874)]
A patient's ABG shows pH 7.25. The expected effect on serum calcium is: [H+ competes for albumin: acidosis increases free Ca; ↓pH 0.1 → ↑Ca 0.1 meq/L. (Book p874)]

elements.source: Daily urinary calcium loss is approximately: [~200 mg lost in urine; 4 mg/kg/24 hours; >4 mg/kg/day = hypercalciuria. (Book p875)]

Match the ‘4/7/11’ stone thresholds — 1) >4 mg/kg/24 hr  2) >7 mg/24 hr  3) <11 mg/kg/24 hr … A) Hyperuricosuria (2nd m/c)  B) Hypocitraturia  C) Hypercalciuria (m/c) [m/c causes of stones: hypercalciuria >4 mg/kg/24 hr (m/c), hyperuricosuria >7 mg/24 hr (2nd m/c), hypocitraturia <11 mg/kg/24 hr. (Book p875)]
Milk-alkali syndrome begins with excess calcium consumption above: [Excess Ca2+ consumption >4 g/day → ↑ paracellular Ca2+ entry. (Book p875)]

In milk-alkali syndrome, hypercalcaemia activates CaSR which then: [Hypercalcaemia (+) CaSR (−) → ↓ Ca2+ absorption and ↓ ADH → volume depletion → RAAS → metabolic alkalosis; also hypercalciuria → stones. (Book p875)]

Match renal calcium handling — 1) PCT  2) TAL  3) DCT … A) 25%, paracellular, PTH-dependent  B) 10%, active transport, most dependent  C) 65%, paracellular, PTH-independent [PCT 65% paracellular independent; TAL 25% paracellular dependent; DCT 10% active transport most dependent. (Book p875)]
A rise in ionized calcium triggers, within SECONDS, the: [Within seconds: parathyroid CaSR (−) PTH release → hypocalcaemia (immediate). (Book p875)]

Within a FEW DAYS, raised ionized calcium acts on the kidney (TAL) CaSR to cause: [Delayed response: kidney (TAL) CaSR (−) Ca2+ reabsorption → hypercalciuria; vice-versa when ionized calcium falls. (Book p875)]
In the TAL diagram, the claudins shown regulating paracellular calcium are: [TAL regulation involves CLDN 16/19 and claudin-14, with PTH raising absorption and CaSR raising excretion. (Book p875)]

elements.source: Match half-lives — 1) PTH  2) Calcitriol  3) 25(OH)D3 … A) 6–8 hours  B) 2–3 weeks  C) 2–4 minutes [PTH 2–4 min; calcitriol 6–8 hours; 25(OH)D3 2–3 weeks (used for blood level estimations). (Book p876)]
The metabolite used for blood-level estimation of vitamin D (longest half-life) is: [25(OH)D3 (2–3 weeks) is used for blood level estimations. (Book p876)]
A GAIN-of-function CaSR mutation causes: [Gain-of-function CaSR → Bartter type V, AD (all other Bartter types AR). (Book p876)]
‘Bartter syndrome type V is autosomal dominant, whereas all other Bartter types are autosomal recessive.’ [Type V AD; all other Bartter types AR. (Book p876)]
In Bartter type V, excessive CaSR activation causes: [Excessive CaSR activation → ↑↑↑ excretion → hypocalcaemia; all other Bartters show hypercalcaemia. (Book p876)]
A LOSS-of-function CaSR mutation (seen in children, AD) produces: [Loss-of-function → FHH, autosomal dominant, seen in children. (Book p876)]
The FHH pathway is: [Failure of CaSR activation → no excretion → complete reabsorption → hypocalciuria + hypercalcaemia. (Book p876)]
